design_detail: Commentary in Public Health Reports (2015) by epidemiologists from the University of Kentucky and ten state or city health departments, writing as members of the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists (CSTE) Overdose Subcommittee, with an illustrative descriptive analysis of 2010 US multiple-cause-of-death (MCOD) data from CDC WONDER for 11 volunteer jurisdictions (Kansas, Kentucky, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, New York City, North Carolina, Oklahoma, Oregon, Utah, Washington) and the United States. Four indicators per jurisdiction: the age-adjusted overdose death rate (ICD-10 underlying cause X40 to X44, X60 to X64, X85, Y10 to Y14); the age-adjusted rate with at least one opioid-analgesic code (T40.2 to T40.4); the age-adjusted rate with T40.6 ('other and unspecified narcotics'); and the crude rate with T50.9 ('other and unspecified drugs') as the only drug code. The indicator values are shown only in a single figure (an image); the text quotes some of them. The work grew out of the CSTE subcommittee's testing of the poisoning-surveillance indicators proposed by the Safe States Alliance Injury Surveillance Workgroup (ISW7). Filed as cross-sectional with the JBI prevalence checklist, as the round brief directs for certificate studies, because the evidence the site would use is the certificate-data comparison; the commentary's arguments and recommendations are recorded separately on this card.
can_establish: That in 2010 US death-certificate data about a quarter of overdose deaths carried no specific drug code, that how often certificates named a drug or drug class differed widely between jurisdictions, and how certifiers' wording maps to ICD-10 codes (a named opioid analgesic to T40.2 to T40.4, 'opioid' alone to T40.6, 'drug overdose' alone to T50.9), which makes drug-specific rates hard to compare between jurisdictions.
cannot_establish: How many of the unspecified deaths involved opioid analgesics, heroin or any other drug (no death was re-examined and no undercount is estimated); whether the type of death-investigation system causes the differences (the system-type percentages are second-hand and unadjusted, and the 11 jurisdictions' systems are not described); or whether the pattern held after 2010 or outside these volunteer jurisdictions.

sample.recruitment: Registry: 2010 MCOD files compiled from death certificates, as made available on CDC WONDER (accessed 16 January 2015) (7th paragraph; Figure, footnote b). Jurisdictions: epidemiologists from 11 jurisdictions volunteered, with members of the CSTE Overdose Subcommittee, to analyse the ISW7 mortality indicators (6th paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Overdose deaths: ICD-10 underlying cause X40 to X44 (unintentional), X60 to X64 (suicide), X85 (assault), Y10 to Y14 (undetermined intent). Drug-specific indicators by multiple-cause T codes as listed in the design detail (7th paragraph and indicator list). The 'unspecified only' indicator counts deaths with T50.9 and no other code in T36 to T50.8.
sample.attrition: Not applicable. Under NCHS rules, rates based on fewer than 10 deaths were suppressed (New York City 'unspecified only'; Kansas and Oklahoma T40.6) and one rate based on fewer than 20 deaths was judged unreliable (North Carolina T40.6); all four were left out of the figure (Figure, footnote a).
sample.selection_effects: The 11 jurisdictions volunteered and were not chosen to represent US states; their death-investigation systems are not described. One year of data (2010), analysed in 2015. Ten of the eleven named authors work in the health departments of jurisdictions they describe; the first author is at the University of Kentucky College of Public Health (Kentucky Injury Prevention and Research Center), and Kentucky had the highest overdose rate and the highest unspecified-only rate quoted in the text.

exposure.measurement: Not an exposure study. The variable of interest is how specifically drugs were named, measured through the ICD-10 multiple-cause codes that NCHS assigns from the certificate text using automated coding software (3rd paragraph). The certifier (coroner or medical examiner) determines the cause of death and completes the certificate; the commentary explains that a named opioid analgesic is coded T40.2 to T40.4, 'opioid' alone T40.6, and 'drug overdose' with no drug T50.9 (3rd and 4th paragraphs). Toxicology is not examined.
exposure.polysubstance: Indicators are not mutually exclusive: a death with an opioid-analgesic code can also carry T40.6 or other codes; only the T50.9 indicator is restricted to deaths with no other drug code (7th paragraph and indicator list).

comparison.controls: Comparison between 11 jurisdictions and the United States on the four indicators; no comparison with toxicology, enhanced surveillance or medical examiner and coroner records. The comparison by type of death-investigation system (centralized state medical examiner against coroner, hybrid and county medical examiner systems) is quoted from earlier work (Warner et al., 2013), not computed here.
comparison.matching: None; overall rates are age-adjusted, but the 'unspecified only' rate is crude because CDC WONDER could not age-adjust that query directly.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable. Jurisdiction characteristics that could explain differences in specificity (investigation system, toxicology practice and funding, caseload, certifier training) are not described or measured.

outcomes.instruments: Age-adjusted rates per 100,000 population (overdose; opioid analgesics T40.2 to T40.4; 'other and unspecified narcotics' T40.6) and a crude rate (T50.9 only), from CDC WONDER queries of 2010 MCOD data (7th paragraph and indicator list).
outcomes.validity_norms: ICD-10 coding by NCHS software is standard; the indicators come from the ISW7 consensus recommendations, which the subcommittee was testing (5th and 6th paragraphs). Agreement of the codes with toxicology is not assessed.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Unspecified' = an overdose death whose only drug code is T50.9; 'opioid analgesic death' = any T40.2 to T40.4 code (T40.2 other opioids, T40.3 methadone, T40.4 other synthetic narcotics); 'other and unspecified narcotics' = T40.6 (4th and 7th paragraphs). Undercounting is inferred from non-specificity; it is not measured.

analysis.effect_sizes: Rates only, without intervals or tests. United States, 2010: 38,329 overdose deaths, age-adjusted 12.3 per 100,000; 16,651 with an opioid analgesic listed (5.4); 9,429 with only 'other and unspecified drugs' (3.0), which is 24.6% of all overdose deaths and agrees with the 'about 25%' quoted from earlier work (editors' arithmetic); opioid-analgesic deaths were 43.4% of the total (editors' arithmetic). Jurisdictions, as quoted in the text: highest overdose rate Kentucky 23.6; highest opioid-analgesic rate Oklahoma 13.6, where only 28 deaths (4%) lacked a specific drug category, so that even if all 28 involved opioid analgesics the rate would rise by less than 1.0; 'unspecified only' rates Kansas 4.2, Michigan 4.8, Kentucky 7.4, Massachusetts and Maryland 0.2 each; T40.6 rates Massachusetts 3.4 and Maryland 1.7 (2nd, 8th and 9th paragraphs). Quoted from Warner et al. (2013): certificates listing specific drugs 92% in states with centralized state medical examiner systems, 62% in decentralized coroner systems, 73% in hybrid systems, 71% in decentralized county or district medical examiner systems (2nd paragraph). The remaining jurisdiction values are in the figure, which could not be viewed.
analysis.covariates: Age adjustment for three of the four indicators only.
analysis.selective_reporting: The text quotes the values that illustrate its argument; the full set is only in the figure. No indicator is given for heroin (T40.1), although the opening paragraph says heroin-related deaths are also undercounted.
analysis.power: Not applicable; several jurisdiction rates were suppressed or unreliable because of small counts.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 2010, a quarter of US overdose deaths had no specific drug code, and jurisdictions differed widely in how often certificates named a drug, a drug class or only 'narcotics': Oklahoma left 4% unspecified, while Kansas, Michigan and Kentucky had unspecified-only rates of 4.2 to 7.4 per 100,000, and Massachusetts and Maryland had few unspecified deaths but many coded only as 'other and unspecified narcotics'. A jurisdiction's drug-specific rate therefore partly reflects how specifically its certifiers write.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The opening paragraph says classification methods may be leading to a substantial undercount of opioid-analgesic and heroin-related deaths, and the 8th paragraph concludes that opioid-analgesic involvement in Kansas, Michigan and Kentucky was “significantly underestimated” (8th paragraph). These are inferences, hedged in the text (possible, even likely; not unreasonable to believe; further study is needed): no death was re-examined, no estimate of the undercount is made, heroin is not analysed, and 'significantly' is not a statistical result. The system-type contrast (92% against 62% to 73%) is relayed from earlier work as the 'degree of underestimation', although it measures specificity, unadjusted. The practical conclusion, to compare jurisdictions on total overdose rates rather than drug-specific rates and to use drug-specific trends only where specificity is stable, follows directly from the data.

timeline.event: Warner, Paulozzi, Nolte, Davis and Nelson, state variation in certifying manner of death and drugs involved (Academic Forensic Pathology; ref 2), the source of the 25% and system-type figures; not indexed in PubMed according to the project's list.
SAMHSA consensus panel's uniform definitions, cited in the commentary as a recommendation not yet consistently adopted (card sc_goldberger_2013, this reader).
Buchanich et al., the effect of incomplete death certificates on estimates of unintentional opioid-related overdose deaths, 1999 to 2015 (title as listed; read by another reader in this round).
NCHS report: the share of US overdose deaths with at least one drug or drug-class code (T36.0 to T50.8) rose from 87.7% in 2017 to 96.0% in 2023 (card sc_garnett_2026, this reader).

replication.where_it_stands: A descriptive illustration, not a study to be replicated. The problem it illustrates, that unspecified certificates hide drug involvement unevenly across jurisdictions, is the subject of later studies on this project's list that re-assign or correct unspecified deaths (for example Buchanich et al., 2018; Ruhm, 2018, by their listed titles; not read for this card). National specificity improved after 2010: in the NCHS data, 12.3% of overdose deaths in 2017 and 4.0% in 2023 had no drug or drug-class code (Garnett et al., 2026), against about a quarter in 2010 here; whether the variation between jurisdictions narrowed is not shown in that report.

funding.affiliations_note: First author at the University of Kentucky College of Public Health (Kentucky Injury Prevention and Research Center); the other ten at the health departments of New York City, North Carolina, Kansas, Utah, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Oklahoma, Washington and Oregon, i.e. the jurisdictions analysed; group authorship by members of the CSTE Overdose Subcommittee. The acknowledgements thank Leonard Paulozzi (CDC) for mentorship and review of the manuscript and Margaret Warner (CDC), an author of the earlier work quoted, for advice on MCOD files. No commercial interest is apparent.

what_would_settle_it: For a sample of overdose deaths coded only T50.9 or T40.6 in several jurisdictions, retrieve the medical examiner or coroner files and toxicology reports, record which drugs were found and judged contributory, and estimate by jurisdiction and investigation system how many opioid-analgesic, heroin and other drug deaths the certificates missed, as the commentary itself proposes.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Complete national vital-statistics data for each jurisdiction and the United States, but the 11 jurisdictions volunteered and are not a sample of US states.
All registered overdose deaths of 2010 in each jurisdiction; no sampling.
National figures rest on 38,329 deaths, but several jurisdiction rates were suppressed (fewer than 10 deaths) or unreliable (fewer than 20), and Oklahoma's unspecified count was 28.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: The 11 jurisdictions' death-investigation systems, toxicology practice and death counts are not described, although the argument turns on how certification practice differs.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: All deaths enter the indicators, but four jurisdiction rates were omitted from the figure under NCHS suppression and reliability rules.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: The condition is the coding itself (overdose by underlying cause; drug specificity by multiple-cause T codes), identified with standard ICD-10 definitions on national data.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Codes are assigned nationally by the same NCHS software; what varies between jurisdictions is the certifier's wording, which is the subject of the paper rather than a measurement flaw.

Standard CDC WONDER rates with NCHS suppression rules, but no intervals, a crude rate set beside age-adjusted rates, and in-text comparisons (more unspecified than opioid-analgesic deaths in Kansas and Michigan) whose basis, counts or rates, is not stated.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response rate managed appropriately

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist, as the round brief directs for certificate studies; the paper is a commentary, so its arguments are recorded under the interpretation gap rather than scored. As a description of how specifically 2010 US certificates named drugs, nationally and in 11 jurisdictions, the data are complete and coded uniformly, but the jurisdictions volunteered, their systems are not described, most values sit in a figure (not viewable in this reading) and there are no intervals. It may be cited for: the 2010 national figures (38,329 overdose deaths; 16,651 with an opioid analgesic coded; 9,429 with only unspecified drugs); the way certifier wording maps to ICD-10 codes; the jurisdiction values quoted in the text; and the CSTE subcommittee's advice that jurisdictions be compared on total overdose rates rather than drug-specific rates. It may not be cited for the size of any undercount, for heroin, or for the effect of investigation-system type, which is second-hand and unadjusted.

key_findings.finding: United States, 2010: 38,329 drug overdose deaths on death certificates (age-adjusted 12.3 per 100,000); an opioid analgesic was listed as contributing in 16,651 (5.4 per 100,000); a further 9,429 (3.0 per 100,000) were associated only with 'other and unspecified drugs'.

Quoted from earlier work (Warner et al., 2013): about 25% of US overdose deaths had no drug specified on the certificate, and the share of overdose certificates listing specific drugs was 92% in states with a centralized state medical examiner system, against 62% with decentralized coroners, 73% with hybrid county coroner and medical examiner systems, and 71% with decentralized county or district medical examiners.
key_findings.note: Second-hand; the years covered and any adjustment are not stated in this commentary.

key_findings.finding: Who decides and who codes: coroners or medical examiners determine the cause of death and complete the certificate; NCHS codes the text to ICD-10 with software that automates and standardizes coding. A death is an overdose death when its underlying cause is X40 to X44, X60 to X64, X85 or Y10 to Y14; T36 to T50 codes identify drug classes.

Wording decides the code: naming an opioid analgesic (for example hydrocodone, methadone or tramadol) gives a code in T40.2 to T40.4; writing 'opioid' alone gives T40.6, 'other and unspecified narcotics'; writing simply 'drug overdose' gives T50.9, 'other and unspecified drugs', and the opioid's contribution disappears from the coded data.

The analysis came from the CSTE Overdose Subcommittee's volunteer testing, in 11 jurisdictions with 2010 certificate data, of the mortality indicators proposed in the Safe States Alliance ISW7 consensus recommendations for poisoning surveillance (April 2012); the subcommittee found limitations in how overdose deaths are counted locally.

Four indicators from 2010 MCOD data on CDC WONDER: age-adjusted overdose death rate; age-adjusted rate with at least one T40.2 to T40.4 code; age-adjusted rate with T40.6; and the crude rate with T50.9 as the only drug code (crude because CDC WONDER could not age-adjust that query directly).

Kentucky had the highest age-adjusted overdose death rate (23.6 per 100,000). Oklahoma had the highest opioid-analgesic rate (13.6), partly because only 28 of its overdose deaths (4%) lacked a specific drug category; even if all 28 involved opioid analgesics its rate would have risen by less than 1.0 per 100,000. 'Unspecified only' rates were relatively high in Kansas (4.2), Michigan (4.8) and Kentucky (7.4), and in Kansas and Michigan more overdose deaths were attributed to 'other and unspecified drugs' than to opioid analgesics.
key_findings.note: The other jurisdiction values are in the figure image, which was not viewable in this reading (the browser pane was hidden and the screenshot came back blank); no value was estimated from it.

key_findings.finding: Massachusetts and Maryland each had few deaths with no drug or class specified (0.2 per 100,000), but substantial rates coded only as 'other and unspecified narcotics' (3.4 and 1.7 per 100,000), which the authors suggest could be opioid analgesic, heroin or cocaine deaths described vaguely as 'opioids' or 'narcotics'.

Rates suppressed under NCHS rules (fewer than 10 deaths): New York City 'unspecified only', Kansas and Oklahoma T40.6; North Carolina T40.6 unreliable (fewer than 20 deaths); all omitted from the figure.

The subcommittee workgroup advises that ranking jurisdictions by drug types named on certificates may mislead, that jurisdictions be compared on total overdose rates, and that drug-specific trends within a jurisdiction remain useful only while the degree of specification does not change markedly from year to year; it suggests checking medical examiner, coroner and toxicology records to identify the drugs in nonspecifically coded deaths.

The commentary cites two 2013 recommendations: that of the National Association of Medical Examiners and American College of Medical Toxicology expert panel, that certifiers list all substances responsible for a fatal overdose on the certificate, and the SAMHSA consensus panel's uniform standards and case definitions for opioid-related deaths. Until these are consistently adopted, the authors write, epidemiologists need to know the quality and limits of their jurisdiction's certificate data, check the completeness and accuracy of the codes where possible, and read counts and rates with caution where the share of deaths with unspecified drugs is considerable; they add that NCHS and some states were working to improve how drugs are specified and that vital-statistics registrars should work with medical examiners and coroners on it.

reporting_issues.issue: The jurisdiction-level indicator values are given only in a figure image; the text quotes a selection (the examples that support the argument).
reporting_issues.consequence: Values not quoted in the text could not be extracted in this reading and cannot be checked from the text.

reporting_issues.issue: The 'unspecified only' indicator is a crude rate while the other three are age-adjusted, and the statement that Kansas and Michigan had more deaths attributed to unspecified drugs than to opioid analgesics does not say whether it compares counts or these differently computed rates.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, 7th paragraph and indicator list; 8th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Cross-indicator comparisons within a state should be cited with that caveat, or as counts from the source data.

reporting_issues.issue: The opening paragraph and the 2nd paragraph say heroin-related deaths are also undercounted, but no heroin indicator (T40.1) is analysed; and the system-type percentages are introduced as the degree of underestimation, although they measure the share of certificates naming a drug.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; indicator list
reporting_issues.consequence: The commentary supports a claim about non-specific certificates, not a measured heroin or opioid undercount.

reporting_issues.issue: No funding or competing-interests statement is printed.
